utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, there's a matter I want to raise just before you begin. Mr. Nice, it came to our attention, in fact you raised it during the ex parte hearing on Friday, but I hasten to say there was no discussion about it since we were in ex parte session, but you very properly raised the matter that as a result of the Defence enquiries about the audiotape, that in fact the exhibits were being retained by the Office of the Prosecutor during this case and copies were being handed over to the Registry. Now, we do not know how this has come about. We understand, from some enquiries, that there may have been a ruling in another case. But clearly it's a matter which must be regularised, because Rule 81(C) states that the Registry should do that, and indeed one would have expected the Rules to say it because, of course, the Court is the proper place to keep the exhibits once they have been produced. Now, I'm not going to interrupt the evidence now that the witness is in court, but at an appropriate moment, clearly we must have a full hearing about this in order to regularise the position and to ensure that we act in conformity with the Rules and the normal conduct of trials as I understand it. In particular, of course, we may have to address some or at least one more controversial exhibit, and it may be necessary to have some evidence about it. But all that we can resolve. But as I said, at an appropriate moment, we will hear you, and of course we will hear the Defence about what the appropriate step should be now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Defence were written to, I think, on Friday, copied to the Chambers, explaining the position in relation to the particular exhibit, and I'm happy to deal with the matter at any convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. We'll ask for the letter, if it's arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, as I say, we'll hear from the Defence on the matter in due course. But we'll also have to consider the Defence exhibits, what the position is about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We've been giving some thought to that, of course, Your Honour, and might I propose this: --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless it's something which is to be dealt with immediately, it may be better if we have a full hearing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, the witness has been detained during this discussion. We'll now begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, and good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would you please state your name for the Court?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: My name is Ivica Kambic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kambic, I'm going to take you fairly quickly through most of the material that's contained in the outline that you have signed. Most of it, I think, is uncontroversial, but if there are any points upon which the Prosecution wishes me not to lead, I would be obliged if they would point that out at the appropriate stage. Some preliminary details, Mr. Kambic. You were born, I believe, on October the 25th, 1950, in Karlovac, Croatia, but your parents moved to Novi Travnik with you when you were just six months old?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You finished your elementary schooling and high schooling in the town of Novi Travnik, attended business school in Sarajevo, but did not take a degree from that institution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that you graduated from the School for Reserve Officers in the JNA and served in the JNA, holding the rank of Captain First Class before you resigned.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that your entire 20-year career was spent at the Bratstvo weapons manufacturing plant in Novi Travnik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that the last position that you held at this factory was as the sales and marketing manager for the department that manufactured armaments and supplies for the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We could not hear the witness. We believe he said, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kambic, I wonder if I might ask you just to approach the microphones a little more closely. Thank you. I believe, sir, that you joined the Croat Defence Council in November of 1992 as a company commander within the 1st Battalion of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, the Novi Travnik Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in April of 1994, you became the Chief of Staff of operations of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, after the Dayton Accords were signed, that is when I was posted to that duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade was reformed and is now called the 90th Home Guard Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: That is what it was called then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And after the civil war ended, sir, I believe that you served in an army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that you held the rank of Captain First Class in the Federation army before your retirement in 1996?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you are currently living in Novi Travnik with your family, your wife, and two children; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: It is. We're all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Kambic, I'd like to turn your attention to the day upon which you and your colleagues were kidnapped, April 13th, 1993. You were engaged in a front line inspection at Kamenjas in the Novi Travnik area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were travelling in an Isuzu four-wheel drive vehicle with three other soldiers, two officers, and a driver; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One of the officers was named Zdravko Kovac and he was a military intelligence officer in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The second officer was Sladjo Sliskovic, a security and information officer?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The driver's name was Miro Jarkovic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: At that time, sir, can you just tell the Court the name of the commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: The commander of the brigade was Colonel Zeljko Sabljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that he had also patrolled the same area earlier that day, but he was driving around in a different vehicle, a Lada Niva?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Correct, a day earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, could you tell the Court, sir, what happened to you as you were intercepted and stopped by a TAM-500 green truck on your way back from the front lines west of Novi Travnik at the Vodovod-Kovacic intersection?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: As we were returning home at that section of the road, Vodovod-Kovacic, the narrowest segment of the road, that green TAM stopped, and where the road is at its narrowest so you cannot overtake it. It stopped and armed soldiers jumped off it, disarmed us, tied us, tied our hands behind our backs, blindfolded us, put adhesive tape over our mouths and put us on to the truck and then took us away. The ride could have taken some 20 minutes, perhaps half an hour, I wouldn't know exactly. I know we stopped and they threw us off the -- took us off the truck and we walked in the snow, because it is in the mountains, probably to the mountains -- no, not probably, they just simply took us to a mountain. There was still snow there. I don't know. At first, I sat against a tree. After a while, one of them took me with him and that was the first interrogation. Who am I, what am I. They took my papers. And at that time, the major problem was my ID because it said my place of birth. As I said, I was born in Karlovac, even though I spent all my life and still live in Novi Travnik. That was normal in the former Yugoslavia because my parents had come from Karlovac looking for jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I can interrupt you for just a minute. Just a matter of detail. We've referred to the front lines that you were patrolling, performing reconnoitering tasks. This is actually the front lines between the Bosnian Serb army on one side and the --

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Us and the Bosnian Serbs. That was the front line between us and the army of Bosnian Serbs at that moment. There was no complaint between us and the BH army. At that time, they held the part of the front which was the continuation -- in continuation of our line or the front against Republika Srpksa, and there were absolutely no signs, no indications that anything like that might happen. So none of us were ready for that, nor did we expect it to happen. We used that territory daily, because Vodovod is a mixed millage. There are both Muslims, Bosniaks, and Croats and Kovacic and other villages in that area are also mixed. So that there were no indications.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just so that the Court has the full picture, sir, do I understand it to be the case that the HVO actually had troops on the front line manning positions against the Bosnian Serb army at the time of your abduction?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes. A unit of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade was daily on that segment of the front line. That unit was usually company strong which is about 100, 150 men on that part on the front on any given day. And the shifts were weekly, that is, one group would be there for a week and then go back and another one would come. At that time, people were still working. It wasn't a permanent army. You go to the front line and then you are free and you go back home and do whatever you do to earn your livelihood, because you had to live off something so that's how we lived at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just to go back a little bit. After you had been dragged out of your car, thrown on the ground, tied up, bound and gagged and driven away, is it the case that the soldiers in the truck in which you were placed beat your colleague Miro Jarkovic several times when he tried to look up?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Absolutely right, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, I believe that after you were taken out of the truck, you were marched to a separate area and then interrogated separately, apart from each other; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Can you just tell the Court about that interrogation process, Mr. Kambic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: There was somebody, I believe he was one of their leaders, a Bosniak. He interrogated us. Afterwards, we learned that he had allegedly attended the mechanical engineering faculty in Belgrade. I don't know if he graduated from it or not. It doesn't really matter. He asked us who we were, what we were, what duties we performed. And after the interview, he fired into the air, not far from my head. And other people, other people thought, I mean those who were not at that interrogation, they thought that they'd killed the one who was being interrogated. That was the first time. The second time when they interrogated us, that one first put his pistol against my forehead and then pushed it into my mouth, presumably wanting me to tell them more than I either knew or could tell him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you beaten at any point during these interrogations?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, a blow here and there on the head with their hand. There was no battery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is it the case, sir, that there were four Mujahedin amongst your kidnappers?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Because the abductors, the Bosniaks, they had mask -- camouflage caps on their heads, and the Mujahedin did not have them because they had no reason to hide their identity, and they told us literally who they were and what they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: During your interrogation--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Sayers. I would like to put a question to the witness. He has just said that the so-called Mujahedin told him or said who they were, where they came from. Could the witness tell us what they said exactly? Where did they come from and what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, they did tell us who they were and what they were. One of them came from Egypt, and before he came to Bosnia-Herzegovina, he used to work as a cook in Milan. Another one came from Tunisia and also used to work in Italy as a goldsmith. The third one came from -- the youngest one came from Saudi Arabia. He lived there and had no job. And the fourth one came from Algeria, came from Algeria.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As the interrogation was going on, sir, did you hear any vehicle noises and could you tell the Court what happened after those noises, if you heard them?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: While this first interrogation went on in the woods, yes, we heard those noises, and then they discontinued the interrogation and took us on foot. I remember they pushed us into a structure, into something solid. We know where it is. It is around Rostovo and there are very many summer cottages there, so they presumably put us in one of those cottages. One could hear the noise of UNPROFOR vehicles, their APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And you were moved, I believe, later that day, after a long march, and ultimately placed into a pillbox?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: We spent the first night in a dugout because there was also the Bosniak army there and they had some facilities there, so that we spent the first night in a dugout. Four nights after that first one we spent in a cowshed, in a sheep -- because there are sheep up there, so we spent four nights in that shed up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And after these four days in the sheep barn, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: And then we were taken to a motel at Ravno Rostovo, and the first time they brought us there, they put us in the attic of that motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would you just tell Their Honours where Ravno Rostovo is located in relation to Novi Travnik, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: The motel at Ravno Rostovo is in the territory of the Bugojno municipality, practically on the boundary between the municipalities of Bugojno and Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe it's actually closer to Bugojno than to Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, absolutely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And is it the case that after you had been taken to the motel, you heard UNPROFOR soldiers or overheard UNPROFOR soldiers again, and the so-called Mujahedin rushed you back to the barn where you had been hidden for the last four days?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then you were brought back to the motel the next day and placed into a room; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is it also correct, sir, that throughout your imprisonment, your captors kept your feet tied together but that your hands were left untied and that you were not actually blindfolded?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No beds were provided to you. Instead, you had to sleep on the floor for the next 30 days of your captivity; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, could you tell the Court about the psychological abuse to which you were subjected, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: From the very first day of our stay there in that room, we immediately had to begin reading the Koran. And during those 30 days, every day at least seven or eight hours were spent discussing with them what we read. We read it aloud, the four of us. We took turns in reading it. And after that, we also had to read other things after those discussions. I read the Hadisa. It is their parables. And I also read Islamic law. And there were all sorts of leaflets and handouts that they used to bring with them. That was the daily routine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Sayers. I'd like to seek some information, some further clarification from the witness. He said that he had to read a couple of things, texts, religious texts. Could the witness tell us in what language he had to read all that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Since members of the BH army were also present in that same building, there was also a translated Koran, and we read the Koran in its translation in our language, and they read it in Arabic because they had the Koran in Arabic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, sir, during your imprisonment and captivity, did you learn anything about the incident or the planning of the incident that resulted in your abduction?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Well, towards the end, before we were exchanged, they told us that they had not been planning to abduct us but rather our commander, and they thought that it was the commander in this better vehicle, the Isuzu. They captured us rather than the commander, because the commander had been to the same front line but he was using a Lada Niva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The commander to whom you're referring is the command of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, Mr. Zeljko Sabljic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did the ABiH soldiers say anything to you during your captivity in connection with how they viewed you as opposed to Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were discussions. At some point, they told us that they hated us Croats; that is, that in fact they disliked Serbs and hated us, the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You've already covered this in response to His Honour Judge Bennouna's questions, Mr. Kambic, but as you were speaking with the Mujahedin that you've identified from the countries that you've identified during the course of your imprisonment, did you find out anything about their plans, their goals or objectives, and if so, could you tell the Court about it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: The Mujahedin were very clear. They came. They said they came here to follow in Alah's road. What does that mean? It means that they were for the Jihad, for the holy war. But since the BH territory negotiations were already being conducted about the cessation of hostilities, they told us at some point that if any peace were reached in the BH territory, they would automatically leave it and go to Somalia, because in Somalia at that time some fighting or something like that had broken out, so that they simply were not interested in any kind of peace in the BH lands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did these people say anything to you about cleansing Bosnia-Herzegovina of Serbs and Croats or not?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: They told us that we could remain in the territory of BiH, but respecting the laws that were in force in the Islamic countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I believe, sir, that these Mujahedin were members of the 7th Muslim Brigade and spoke in respectful terms about it, while speaking somewhat condescendingly about the armed forces of the ABiH generally.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And who was their commander, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade at that time was Mahmut Karlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about him?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Based on what they said, I don't know him. But before the war, Mr. Mahmut Karlic was a religious teacher. He was a teacher at the Medresa in Sarajevo before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just move on to the next subject for the Court, paragraph 29 of the outline. Did you know Dario Kordic, who is one of the accused in this case, sir, during the war?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I personally never met him. I just knew him from sight, but never met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What did you know about him?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I knew that he was vice-president of the HDZ-BiH, that he was a politician, and nothing else in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Was he a soldier, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever see him on TV shows wearing camouflage clothing at all?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I did not see him on television wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just generally, though, sir, in the civil war, is it the case that most people were wearing some sort of camouflage clothing or pieces of camouflage clothing?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: That was usual. Even children were wearing them. All adult men practically were wearing these camouflage uniforms or uniforms during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you or your brigade, as far as you're aware, ever receive any orders from Mr. Kordic of any kind, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: If there were any orders, I was not in a position to know about it and I didn't know. I could have received orders only from my immediate commander, that is, the battalion commander, and he then, in turn, could have received it from his commander, Mr. Zeljko Sabljic, and I don't know whether there were any orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Mr. Sabljic, in the chain of command, reported to the Operative Zone commander, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the Operative Zone commander, in turn, reported to the General Staff located variously in Posusje, Mostar, and Grude; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You yourself never received an order from Mr. Kordic, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever heard that Mr. Kordic ever issued or tried to issue military orders to people who were in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to the final subject I'd like to cover with you, Mr. Kambic, and it concerns trench-digging. In Novi Travnik in April of 1993, men of military age who were unable to go to the front lines or had other --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps this oughtn't be led completely. We ought to get the witness's source of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's perfectly acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe for the Judges, Mr. Kambic, what kind of obligations, if any, men of military age had who were not actually fighting on the front lines in the Novi Travnik area?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question for me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did men of military age who were not actually serving as soldiers have any work obligations as far as you are aware or not?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did have work obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Can you just describe to the Court what kind of obligations those were, Mr. Kambic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Within the brigade, we had work platoons and their task was to dig military fortifications, dugouts. They were not -- there were people who would not be in the trenches and carry weapons. That was the usual practice at that time. At that time in Novi Travnik, anybody -- everybody was engaged in some way. They had to contribute in some way in order for us to be able to defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And the last subject I would like to cover with you concerns the solitaire number one building in Novi Travnik in autumn of 1993. Did you ever hear of situations where Muslims had forced Croats in the town of Novi Travnik and surrounding villages to dig trenches in the vicinity of that building, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything else about the efforts to capture this building and what it was used for in the autumn of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: This building was inhabited but Muslim civilians occupied it, but it was located closer to our line, the line we covered and the -- both the ABiH and our side tried to gain control of this building, and since it was closer to us, they were forced to dig. There is a department store in that area so they dug from the department store to the building across the street in order to reach that building and this was done by the captured Croats from Senkovici, Kovacici, Gornje and Donje Pecine. These were brothers or fathers of soldiers who were with me and they were -- they looked on, but we were faster and we captured the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I appreciate it, but for the Court's information, we have a witness from Senkovici scheduled to testify later in the week so perhaps it would be better to cover that subject with him rather than take up valuable time with this witness. After that building had been captured, did you find anything in there of military interest?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Oh, we discovered weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What kinds of weapons?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Rifles and pistols.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did any of the rifles have telescopic sites on them?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I personally did not see these weapons because it was taken to the brigade headquarters so I wouldn't know whether there were any sniper rifles there, but there were weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were any civilians killed in the action to capture this high-rise building as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No, nobody was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, Mr. Kambic. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kambic, my name is Bozidar Kovacic. I represent Mr. Cerkez along with my colleague Mr. Mikulicic, and we would like to ask you several questions now that you are giving evidence here, and this would refer to Mr. Cerkez's Defence. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber when you met Mario Cerkez who is present here?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I met Mr. Mario Cerkez on the occasion when I joined the HVO. When I joined the HVO, Mr. Boro Malbasic was commander and Mr. Mario Cerkez was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You are referring to the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade had its headquarters in Novi Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This brigade was a joint brigade, it was composed of both Novi Travnik and Vitez municipalities' population?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The brigade was of -- established in November 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you joined it immediately?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You became a company commander?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: While Malbasic was brigade commander, do you know exactly what position Mr. Cerkez had?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, Mario was in charge of holding the line against the troops of the Serbian army and by his duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And by his duty he was the second man in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Malbasic was transferred in February 1993 and Mr. Cerkez became number one in the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And at that time, your only objective and your only task is combat against the Bosnian Serbs in the area which you described as Kamenjas, Slatka Vodica, Mravinjac and the areas you described?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And do you -- and now just to conclude with this topic, do you know that Mr. Cerkez had been transferred to Vitez and then he left to go and take over there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: After Cerkez left, the commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade became Zeljko Sabljic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And Zeljko Sabljic was a member of the command while Cerkez was there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Zeljko Sabljic at that time was the chief of engineers?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that he worked with Cerkez in order to improve the fortifications and defence lines against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I recall, they were working on it and I think that they did what was needed in terms of engineer's work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the period that we were discussing now which is between November of 1992 until early -- that is until the -- what you referred to as the third conflict, that is, April of 1993, were there any serious conflicts between the Muslims and Croats, between the two opposing sides in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I believe that occasionally there were incidents. You would agree with me?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But generally speaking, we could call it a status quo following the cease-fire which was reached in late 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know, as an HVO officer, that at that time or at any other time, for that matter, there was an official or unofficial policy of persecution of the Muslim population in the territory where you were active?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard that anybody incited anyone to persecute another ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The defence against the BSA north-west of Novi Travnik in the sector which we described in 1992 started even before the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade was established.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And it continued after the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade was established, that is through -- in 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know until when in -- who -- were there groups or individuals from Vitez present there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Until the conflict between us and the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean the open conflict in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know, that is, when this conflict broke out, you had your regular shifts up there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And there was a shift from Novi Travnik in the sector which was manned by the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade and there was a shift from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had a company there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many people from Vitez were there at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I don't know but our company was about 150 strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the Vitez Brigade held a sector which was also manned by one company.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: It could have been a company or something else, because at that time, I did not have contacts with the Vitez Brigade at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But they were on your flank; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And on the 16th of April, 1993, when the conflict broke out, this group whose size you don't know, was at the front line?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You know this from your personal observation?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, because my own unit was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: They were flanking you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Since we are at the -- discussing this front line, let me just take you further there. People were there in shifts?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: They spent their eight to ten days and then they would go back home.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When they were on the shift up there, they were considered soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If they commit any criminal acts, who would you call, being a commander, what type -- what kind of police would you call?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When they go back home, are they considered civilians or are they still soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And he goes to work in a factory if he was there employed?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, he would go back to his regular job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So if he was a farmer, he would go back to farm?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The small arms weapons used at the front line against the BSA for the most part remained there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: At that time, we were not fully armed so part of the weapons remained up there and was rotated. One shift would leave weapons to the next shift and would come back home without weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When the third conflict started in April 1993, a lot of weapons stayed behind at the front line.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: At the time when the conflict between the ABiH army -- ABiH started, there was a lot of weapons and a lot of ammunition which was there, much more than they had in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Novi Travnik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On the basis of information which you have, was the case similar with the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: It is possible, but I don't have exact information on what they had at the time. I can tell you more precisely what we had at our front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You don't know but you know that they had the same system operating?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about meetings of the senior representatives of both sides, that is HVO and ABiH in November 1992 at a time when Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade was established when the defence was -- with the reference improved the defence or even to go on the offensive when Jabanice Boharat Cusic [phoen] was there. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was not yet with the HVO but I heard from my colleagues that there were negotiations after the second conflict to set up a joint command that would include ABiH and the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade. At that time, the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade had -- was headquartered in the so-called "old hotel" and I know that my colleagues said that -- told me that offices had already been allocated for the ABiH officers to join this command, but that never came through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that some senior ABiH officers, some ranking officers who were with the Croatian army that were -- they were training with the Croatian army before they joined the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I know there were soldiers, people who were with the HV units at that time when the conflict broke out between the JNA and the defending forces and that -- but they returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were these BiH citizens who had temporarily worked or lived in Croatia where they found themselves when the aggression of the Serbs started?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And when the conflict in Bosnia started, they came back home?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: My colleague Vlado Sliskovic worked in Croatia. This is where he found himself when he was -- when the war broke out. He was in a special unit in Lucko, and then after the conflict broke out, he came back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Lucko, and just to confirm it for the Trial Chamber, Lucko is near to Zagreb. Very well, just a few more things in order to understand the situation. The 308th ABiH army was headquartered in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, Bislim Zurapi was the commander of it during the time that Cerkez was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: He was an Albanian from Kosovo, a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he is an officer in Kosovo with the main headquarters?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No, but after -- but after this cease-fire, I know that he was -- I had contact with him for a while. He was in Denmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- is it true to say that you considered him a correct commander?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And while you were there, you could talk about cease-fires and so on?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received an order and I shot and Zeljko Sabljic received orders and he shot. This is what military officers do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From other local senior ABiH officers there, there were none others whom you considered to be correct.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if the usher could kindly move that overhead projector so Mr. Kambic can see me if he wants to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you help us, please, about when you first arrived in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you first arrive here in Holland?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: First time in Holland? This is the first time in my life that I am actually in the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you come here? Last week?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I arrived on Saturday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to talk to Mr. Kovacic, the man who's just been asking you questions before you came in here to give evidence today?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, I'm in no position to accept in detail or to challenge what happened to you in your kidnapping. I acknowledge that what you tell us is a very distressing story. What I want you to do is help us with one exhibit, please, which is our 941. I don't think you speak English, do you, Mr. Kambic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, what we'll do is put this document on the overhead projector and I'll go through it sufficiently slowly, and I just want your comments on its overall accuracy. It's a summary prepared by one of the international observers at the time, and it sets out the whole chronology of history of the kidnapping and the exchange and I just want you to tell us if it's accurate, that's all. So we -- just so that you can know what we're looking at, we're looking at part of a report that was prepared on the 19th of May by some European monitors and paragraph one makes it clear that between the 16th of February and the 11th of April, -- I'm sorry -- in early April, some 11 citizens from different Arabian countries had been arrested by HVO police together with either one or two local drivers. Is that accurate, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what we were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then on the 14th of April, the four of you were arrested on your return from the front line, as you've described, followed on the 16th of April by the arrest of Mr. Tosic -- or not the arrest, the kidnapping of Mr. Tosic, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The report goes on to say that tension between the parties rose, but you at that time, of course, were in detention, so you wouldn't know, necessarily, what was happening in the area; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I only know what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It does go on to say that Zenica was shelled by HVO artillery. Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you know that the shelling was by the HVO; yes?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then on the 19th of April, it says that messengers, Mujahedin messengers, went to the Hotel Internacional and told European Monitors that they held Mr. Tosic and you, the four of you, and they claimed also to hold five other HVO soldiers arrested in Zenica on the 17th and 18th of April. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that they threatened, according to this report, that unless HVO foreigners -- I beg your pardon -- unless foreigners held by the HVO were released, they would start to kill their hostages. Did you hear anything about that sort of threat being made?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I did not hear anything except for what they told us up there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to go to paragraph 7. The European Monitors offered to mediate, and they were seeking lists of names of everyone to be exchanged and seeking ICRC access to prisoners and hostages to guarantee that everyone was alive who was said to be held, and the Mujahedin rejected the idea of an ICRC visit and proposed an exchange of letters and videotapes. Does that fit with your recollection of events?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were letters exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then there was another message -- paragraph 8 -- by the Mujahedin, in which they listed 15 detainees altogether, and they wanted back confiscated cars; they sent a letter from Mr. Tosic -- Tokic, and so on. Would you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next thing that this chronology of events sets out is that Mr. Blaskic -- Colonel Blaskic was prepared to release foreign detainees kept in Kaonik in return for the five HVO officers, he saying that that was the total number of people he had under his control. Did you know anything about Blaskic offering a release at a fairly early stage?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know anything that stood in the way of Blaskic's offer being acted on at that stage?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this stage, the chronology says the message went -- or the offer, as it were, went to the 3rd Corps, who denied any relationship with extremists and involvement in the kidnapping, and they suggested that the Mujahedin were out of control. Did you hear anything about people saying the Mujahedin were out of control, certainly so far as the 3rd Corps were concerned?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then there's a reference to the liaison soldier from the 7th Muslim Brigade, and they were informed about the proposal as well, and there was a discussion about the exchange, some involvement of the local radio station. The 7th Muslim Brigade were visited later. He denied any relationship with the extremists but did ask the ECMM for a meeting, and it's worth noting that the car of the Mujahedin messenger was seen in the headquarters there. And then letters from your officers were provided. Do you remember roughly how long it was after your initial kidnapping that the letters were provided, and I think an audiotape as well?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: We did not receive any letter or any videotape. We sent our letters to our people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My mistake. That's what I was intending. Do you remember roughly how long it was after your detention or kidnapping that you provided letters?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd day, that is, when each one of us sent one letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then apparently the HVO rejected the proposal to sit with the Mujahedin but accepted a proposal to meet with the ABiH, UNPROFOR, ICRC, and ECMM. Did you know anything about the HVO rejecting the proposal to sit with the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We then learn that the Monitors warn the 3rd Corps that they were going to be responsible for the Mujahedin, uncontrolled elements or not. And if we turn over to paragraph 19 -- I hope I'm not missing out anything anybody else wants me to put in -- on the 11th of May a messenger from the Arab group, as he called himself, proposed to the ECMM the release of the five officers, the two men from Radio CD on the one side and 11 prisoners from the Arabian countries on the other side, and the proposal was that it would be done on three different sites. Does that fit with your recollection of events? In fact, it happened on the 12th of May, the exchange itself. I beg your pardon. It didn't happen. It was going to happen on the 12th, but it didn't finally happen until the 17th. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were exchanged on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the exchange in Zenica was associated with a crowd of Mujahedin supporters or similar cheering and making a somewhat threatening presence. Did you see anything of that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I could not see anything, because I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Did you hear about it? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But other than the things that you didn't see or hear because you weren't there, that summary of events by the Monitors at the time would appear to be accurate, would it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you don't point to anything in it that's inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I cannot say whether it is or is not accurate, because I did not see any of that, nor was I -- nor did I have an opportunity to see that. I can only tell you what we did up there and what they asked us to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a couple of other things, really. Do you remember a man called Ismet Halilovic, who in February of 1993 was attacked by some HVO soldiers in your command? Do you remember about that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the Judges have heard a bit about this, so we needn't go into the detail too much. Although there was the beginning of a court hearing into the attack on him, it never came to anything, and is the position this: that although these men were in your command, you didn't yourself take any disciplinary action against them?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I don't understand that "you". Do you mean me or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, you personally.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I can't see any role for me in all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was your relationship to these men? Were you their commander?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I was the commander of the company in company of the escorting company at that moment, and they were not members of that escort company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I thought you said they were in your command when I asked you a few minutes ago. But tell us what the position is.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No, I did not say that. They were in the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, but not in my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because you'll remember that the man himself, Halilovic, suffered seriously with a gunshot through the head or neck, although he survived it, and his brother was killed and so on. And the soldiers, one of them was wearing a Ustasha badge on his cap, that sort of thing. Why weren't they disciplined, please?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: You should ask my superior commanders about that. I can't tell you anything more about that because I simply had no responsibility, no powers to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To whom should we address that query, specifically?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I suppose his commander, or the brigade commander, or the head of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any names you can give us? He's only named you, I think, as the commander, you see.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I can tell you who was the commander at the time, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that was?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: It was Zeljko Sabljic, he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Going back in time to October 1992, you were in Novi Travnik then?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have anything to do with the consequences of a blockade near Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You heard of a blockade near Ahmici on about the 19th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: At that time, at that point in time, I did not use that particular part of the road, and there were roadblocks all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you have any part to play in a meeting at the Territorial Defence headquarters where Cerkez appeared, the topic of the meeting being the blockade near Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No. At that time, I was not -- I had not joined the HVO at that time yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to trouble with any more detail, just these points, then. You said something about the Mujahedin, who kidnapped you, being members of the 7th Muslim Brigade. Is this what they told you, or is this what you worked out for yourself, or what?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: They told us so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so far as the digging of trenches is concerned, is that something you observed yourself or something you were told about?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: What kind of trenches do you mean, the trenches that the HVO dug or towards the skyscraper?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You tell us. It's the ones, I think, that you say were dug in Novi Travnik in April of 1993. Did you see any of that yourself?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Well, trenches were dug all around in Travnik. When the conflict broke out, then trenches were dug along all the front lines, wherever it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're saying something about people who were on the front line on the 16th of April of 1993 coming from Vitez. I didn't quite understand it. Who is it you say were on the front line on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, on the front line against the army of Republika Srpska, there was the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade unit and there was also a unit of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And can you name the Vitez Brigade or give us any detail of who it was from the Vitez Brigade there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot give you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did you learn anything about what was happening elsewhere in Central Bosnia on the 16th of April, what was happening in Ahmici, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: As to what had happened in Ahmici, we learned about that while we were in captivity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But at the time on the 16th of April, you learned nothing of what was happening elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what were you told? You might as well complete the story. What were you told in captivity about what had happened in Ahmici, so that we can have the full story?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: They told us that units -- some HVO units had attacked Ahmici and that civilians had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you identify the units?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot do that because I was not there, and that is all that I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Two short matters, Mr. Kambic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Throughout the 35 or so days of your captivity, was the Red Cross ever allowed to meet with you and register you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The second question concerns one of the questions that you were asked about by the Prosecution concerning an incident on April the 19th of 1993 in which the city of Zenica was shelled. You were in captivity, obviously, on the 19th; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You don't have any personal knowledge at all about that shelling incident, do you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KAMBIC
utterances.text: I couldn't. I told you what happened in Zenica. That is what we were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kambic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The next witness is Josip Buha, but I don't believe he's scheduled to arrive until 11.00, Your Honours. So if we may, could we take an early break? But let me just alert the Court that there is an affidavit, a short affidavit, of Mario Santic that we have filed prior to the testimony of Mr. Buha which corroborates or is submitted in corroboration of the specific facts upon which he had been brought to court to testify about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the next witness is called, can I say something as well? I've received all the witness summaries this morning for the first time. I think they were eventually faxed at 4.15 yesterday afternoon, and although there were people working here over the weekend, the last search produced none of them when they went home. There has been a complete change of order from what was anticipated, and I'm certainly not in a position to cross-examine the next witness, Buha, now, and it may well be, because I had forecast his arriving much later in the week, I won't be in a position to cross-examine him properly or adequately today at all. I can only go so far, and I have to work on the forecast listing of witnesses, so that's my position at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And will you help us about this, Mr. Sayers? Is it right that on the list, he's at the very bottom of one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, but I think the Prosecution knows exactly what Mr. Buha has been brought to talk about, because it was in our summaries that we filed some weeks ago in conformity with the Court's order. Unfortunately, we had some travel difficulties with our witnesses, and that's resulted in our having to shuffle the order slightly. And we have provided the Prosecution with a copy of the outline that was signed by Mr. Buha as soon as he signed it. We faxed it over to the Prosecution's office yesterday, along with two others for the witnesses that we plan to call today, Mr. Kambic included, and Mr. Pavlovic, the third witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: His name appears right at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I apologise for having to do this. There's no tactical considerations that have been present in this, it's just the situation that we are presented with. And I might say, Your Honour, that this happened to the Defence on a fairly regular basis, and we never once asked for cross-examination to be deferred. We just went ahead and cross-examined, with the exception of the very earliest days, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure it's right to say you never asked for it. But we'll have to consider this in due course. Who have you got, so we can follow the position? You've got Mr. Buha, and he will be here at 11.00 or for 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got Mr. Pavlovic. Where is he at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He's scheduled to arrive at 2.30, but we could probably have him here earlier, if necessary. The next witnesses after that would be the Kakanj witnesses, [name redacted] and [name redacted], but their outlines have not been signed yet. We still have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They are here, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We've made an application for protective measures, so I wonder if we could delete from the record the second witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But they are here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They are here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And your proposal is to call them tomorrow or as soon thereafter as possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. The witness after that is Major Franjo Ljubas, and he's also here, but we don't have a signed summary from him yet, although we hope to have one later today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What does he deal with?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He deals with Travnik, the fighting around Travnik, and the command structure in the Travnicka Brigade from the lower level. And the two final witnesses are Mr. Zlatan Civcija, who deals with the political situation in Novi Travnik, and he is here and currently working on his outline. We don't have a signed copy of that yet. And then finally (redacted) (redacted), and he is, I believe, coming in later this evening, but he is not here yet. In fact, he was the gentleman that caused our difficulty. It turns out that he actually didn't have a passport, and so interim arrangements had to be made, and that caused us to shuffle the order of all of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I need to say this: The problem with the witness Buha is we deal with the summary to which Mr. Sayers refers. That's the early summary. The summary is entirely general and simply says Mr. Buha will discuss the circumstances under which Mr. Breljas became a member of the Vitezovi and will testify about the meeting of April the 15th and will explain that Mr. Kordic wasn't present. There's no way I can prepare for any cross-examination on the basis of that sort of summary. I had made a provisional arrangement to be in a position to deal with the detail of Buha later in the week, assuming that I was going to be provided with a summary later in the week. And I just simply may not have been in the position, despite taking every step I could this morning, to be adequately informed to cross-examine on the detail of the statement that's now provided. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll consider any application you make on the matter. You know the position, that we are extremely anxious to get on with this case. And it is right, as Mr. Sayers said, that the Defence indeed did, after initial applications, cross-examine when people came in, and I'm afraid we shall have to expect the same of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I've been doing it, despite the difficulties, and I no doubt will do it. But I've made the point that if I can't cross-examine on something, I'm not going to do either a token cross-examination or go in general terms for somebody's credibility when I don't know, one way or another, whether I should be accepting or rejecting what he says. So that's our difficulty, and of course if things are left unresolved in cross-examination, there may always be the possibility of rebuttal. But that's less fair and it's less satisfactory if the matter hasn't been cross-examined to first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you've heard our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: May I? [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, what do you mean in relation to this witness, Mr. Buha, Josip Buha? Do you think that the summary you've been provided with is inefficient? Do you therefore somehow fear that the Defence would go further than what has been stated in that summary? That is, if I've got you right and that you were duly informed, these are very specific -- very precise items. We are talking about the possible presence of Mr. Kordic at that meeting of the 15th of April, 1993. The remainder is basically a recurrent issue. It is part of the Defence strategy, which is to know whether Mr. Kordic has had any military authority or not. So you say that you are not prepared for that, but you've cross-examined on several occasions on that item. The outstanding item is precise, and that is why the witness is called. So you should be prepared for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The only point I was making touched on neither of those topics but on the topic of the details of Breljas' arrival in the brigade, and that's the matter for which there is no detailed forecast. That's the matter which I forecast I might need to have some assistance with and for which I've made plans for later in the week. I've tried to accelerate the plans, and I shall find out, no doubt in the interval, in the break, as I should describe it, how far those plans are. But the other topic about Kordic not being at the meeting, I knew I was going to have to meet that, of course, and the general topics. But it's the Breljas detail that's beyond me to deal with in detail at the moment, and it may be important; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now. Half past 11.00, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Buha, be so kind to introduce yourself with your full name to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Josip Buha.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Buha, you were born on 14 March in 1954 in Buhine Kuce in the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You are a carpenter by profession, but at the present, you are working for a private company clearing mines?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You are a team leader that includes Croats, Muslims, and Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You are married, you have three children and a grandson?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Your entire family lives in the village of Dubravica in the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Buha, a few words about your military service to call it that way. You were a member of the Croat Armed Forces, HOS?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You became a member of the HOS and HOS is a military arm of the Croatian Party of Rights at the very beginning, that is, in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Who was your HOS commander in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: My commander was Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Your house unit in September of 1992 was in a way incorporated into the HVO, the Croat Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And from 10 September 1992 your unit was renamed the Special Purpose Unit of Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Your commander continued to be Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Buha, both at the time when you were with the HOS and with the Vitezovi unit, your basic job was logistics. You were the logistics person for those units?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber where in 1992 your unit was deployed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: It was actually accommodated in the elementary school in Dubravica. And the HVO units were at the fish pond in Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So these PPN -- Vitezovi used the Dubravica school as some kind of a provisional barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Buha, the Trial Chamber has already heard about alleged meetings held on 15 April 1993. I would like to ask you to tell the Trial Chamber whether on 15 April 1993, any meeting was held in the afternoon or evening attended by any politicians including say Mr. Kordic or any other politician?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: On that date, no meeting took place. Nobody attended it, and especially it was not attended by Mr. Kordic or any politician from Vitez or beyond.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You are aware of the fact that Ante Breljas -- that this meeting took place on the evening of that date, the 15th of April and that he attended it, that is Mr. Breljas?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: As I said, there was no meeting and it could not have been and it did not happen on the 15th of April and Ante Breljas was not present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: On 15 April, you spent the entire day in the elementary school of Dubravica, that temporary barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Like all other days, I was in the school the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Had anyone outside of your unit or some civilian, one of the politicians who had come to the barracks, would you have known about it or would you have heard or seen it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes. I would have had to have seen it or heard it. The duty officer would inform me about it and I would show up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: This was a relatively small barracks, small compound.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes, relatively small.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you said that Ante Breljas could not have been at a meeting for which you say never took place on the 15th of April, but you say that he was not in the elementary school in Dubravica on the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes, I continue to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Can you then please tell the Trial Chamber when, on what date did you see for the first time the person who later was identified as Ante Breljas?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I saw this gentleman on -- at around 1400 hours on the 16th. That is, the next day I saw him, on the 16th around 1400 hours in the Dubravica school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When you say the 16th, you're referring to 16 April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes, 16 April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you know where this gentleman was arrested on that day, that is when he was seen for the first time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's been no evidence that he was arrested. Now, the simplest thing is to ask the witness what were the circumstances in which he saw Mr. Breljas that day. Can you tell us that, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Of course I can say. I saw him on that day in the school among the soldiers and he was -- he had been arrested by the gas station called "Hvidra". That is its current name. He was arrested under unusual, strange circumstances and he was brought to the school. He was being watched by the soldiers around him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Naumovski. Mr. Naumovski, excuse me. I should like to ask the witness, he says that he was arrested under strange circumstances which were not quite normal. Could the witness explain what he means by that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain it. Because it was not possible at that time for him to be there, because there were combat operations going on so he was immediately detained and brought to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no further questions, Your Honour, I would go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let me follow up on this, Mr. Buha. He was a suspect because he was caught in these circumstances and so he was brought to the school.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: That is exactly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Breljas stayed detained or under watch in the school at Dubravica for a while, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But after this period of time when he was under observation, he became then a member of the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: What led to this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: It was his own way of flattery, and also his knowledge of English so he endeared himself to the commander so to speak, and became a member of the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So whom did he flatter?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: It was mostly Mr. Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: After Mr. Breljas became a member of Vitezovi, where did he work at first?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: He at first worked with me in the logistics department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: After a while, he joined the IPD. He worked for the IPD.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
