utterances.text: Thank you. We will come back to these questions later, but I just want to close this topic regarding these meetings. Was any meeting held on the 16th of April, 1993 in the afternoon where some of the politicians may have attended?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: There was no meeting there. We were already deployed in areas where there were -- fighting was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So at that time, you were no longer in the barracks; is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No, at that time we were no longer in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You were with a special-purpose unit. You spent the entire time in the Vitez area, and you must have heard about Mr. Kordic. You had some knowledge about him?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Can you please say, looking from your point of view and based on your knowledge, was Mr. Kordic a politician or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic was only a good politician. He was no soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Throughout the time when you were with the Vitezovi PPN and you spent the -- you were with them from September 1992 until the middle of January 1994. Throughout the existence of the Vitezovi unit, you were with them, and have you at any time heard that Mr. Kordic tried to or did issue an order to the Vitezovi PPN?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No such order ever came to the Vitezovi from anyone, and especially not Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: As a member of Vitezovi, whose orders did you exclusively follow?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I exclusively followed the orders of my commander, Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Could anyone else other than Darko Kraljevic issue orders to you or the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No, and I would not receive it from anyone else but Mr. Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this will conclude my questioning, and I want to thank Mr. Buha.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Buha. Let me introduce myself. I'm Bozo Kovacic. I represent Mr. Mario Cerkez, alongside Mr. Mikulicic, and I would just like to follow up on what you have stated so far. [In English] Your Honour, there is an error in the transcript on page 50, line 22, second sentence, where the witness clearly says "HOS units were in Kruscica," and the transcript said "HVO".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Buha, first of all, I will follow up on the issues we discussed -- you discussed with Mr. Naumovski. Could Darko Kraljevic issue any orders to Mario Cerkez, and had he done so, would he have accepted them?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Regarding the correction in the transcript, HOS and later Vitezovi were in Kruscica, and Darko lived in Rijeka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This is the area where you moved about?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, on the eve of the conflict in April 1992, that is, on the 13th of April, did ABiH members try to assassinate Mr. Darko Kraljevic in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And is it true that a Batian [phoen] soldier was there with Mr. Kraljevic and Niko and Jakov Krizanac?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But they managed to escape?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes, but the equipment and vehicles were captured by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether after that, Mr. Darko sent a letter, a protest letter, to the command of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buha, can you recall whether a member of your unit had a nickname Cano? Can you identify this person for us?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, who it was?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes. His name is Franjo, and his last name is Sapina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean Franjo Sapina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: He was also a member of the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And he was from Donja Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just a couple of questions regarding a document. Can I please have the Registry provide us with the Exhibit Z2332.1. This is from the so-called Spork batch. [In English] Could you please put it in front of the -- or maybe on the ELMO, and then the witness could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please tell me, do you know anything about the list of all military personnel of the Vitezovi unit regarding some monetary compensation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this. Was Drago Vinac Darko Kraljevic's deputy?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know when he joined the Vitezovi? Was it summer or spring?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Approximately between -- the 1st of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you look at this list, please? [In English] First page of the text after this cover page. Yes. [Interpretation] Can you identify Drago Vinac? He's listed under "2"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes, I can see him listed as number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If you now look to the next column, according to this data, he joined on the 8th of April, 1992, it would seem. Is that correct or is it correct what you said, that he joined much later, significantly later?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly. I believe that what I have stated previously -- I don't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about all members of -- that the period of active duty with the HVO was blown out of proportion, if I may use that, in order for them to gain more compensation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I have not heard of such stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is your father's name Ilija?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Usher, would you be so kind as to try to locate the page where you have the numbers "16/96"? That is about in the middle of the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Buha, while we're searching for it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let the usher find it. Whereabouts is the figure "16/96" to be found on the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the middle of the page, and the middle of the material is the page [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there not -- I see. Is there no page numbers on the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, unfortunately not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be simplest if you hand the usher your copy, rather than him having to try and find it, and we'll put that on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We now discovered there was an error in the transcript. I said the numbers lined on the paper, not the page numbers, as is what's translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got it now, "16/96".

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I marked this entry. Does this refer to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And also your personal number corresponds to your number?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Further right, it's not on the screen -- [previous translation continues] ... [In English] He can see the right side of the page. Right. Okay, perfect. [Interpretation] And you can see here that your date of entry is 22nd of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In that period which was entered here, you were a member of the HOS, which later was transformed into Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. You were never a member of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more detail, if I can use your presence for some further persons. But let me ask you this. Do you know that a colleague of yours had a nickname of Tasko?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you recall Marko Mlakic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Marko Mlakic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know that perhaps, by his close friends and associates, he was called Tasko?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the usher would like to hand back that document to Mr. Kovacic and perhaps return the other one to the Registry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that, Your Honour, concludes my testimony -- my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I made my position clear earlier. It may be that I'd be in a better position later to conclude what I should ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't you make a start now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can certainly make a start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And see how we get on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't want to pad up by using time because I suspect that the other material I want won't be here until lunchtime or after.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Buha, just let me check whether you'd agree with the following: The Vitezovi were a special unit formed on the 10th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, do you have your next witness available or is he not here until 2.00 or something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Not here until 2.30, unfortunately. Do you want me to make inquiries whether we can accelerate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It might be, yes, because what I have in mind is if the cross-examination concludes before 1.00, we might usefully spend the time hearing the next witness, and we'll have to consider whether to allow the Prosecution the adjournment to look through their voluminous documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With the Court's permission then, if our paralegal can go make the appropriate inquiries, that should be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Vitezovi was a special unit formed on the 16th of September 1992. They wore black uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No, Vitezovi were not formed. When black uniforms were worn on the 22nd of November, 1991, that was HOS which was founded and then they wore black uniforms. And on the 10th of September, we became a Special Purpose Unit called Vitezovi. That's when we were formed and that's when we were called Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am summarising before you what I think has been given as a judgement in another case, and I just want your comments on it. Is it the case that sometimes HVO soldiers also wore black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes, depended what you -- what was available. That's what you wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so by the time of Ahmici, there were still some HVO soldiers still wearing black uniforms in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And therefore, the sight of somebody in a black uniform could be ambiguous, it might identify an HVO soldier, it might identify a policeman and earlier on it might have identified HOS. Is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Perhaps, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Blaz Kraljevic, what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened to Blaz Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Got killed. I don't know the circumstances exactly, I just know that the man was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who killed him; do you know?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who wanted him killed; do you know?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time he was killed, was there pressure to make HOS become subject to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And he stood out against it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I don't understand, who was against it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Blaz was against it.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly after his death, HOS became part of the HVO, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And at the time, his death was connected with the transfer of authority?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: HOS was founded on the 10th of September, which was when HOS was converted into the Special Purpose Unit. Not because the said gentleman died.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Blaz was also a person who wanted good relations with the Muslims, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And by the time HOS had become a Special Purpose Unit, that desire for good relations with the Muslims had become a thing of the past, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Not true. There were -- effort was already made to establish great cooperation and go together to fight against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's deal with one detail I can deal with at the moment and it's this: There was in Dubravica a coffee house called "The Kruscica"; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Not a coffee shop, a restaurant. Yes, Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You visited that coffee house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes. That's our mess, our canteen where the kitchen for the troops was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Kordic visit that coffee house?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No, I never saw him there. Even though I went there three or four times a day on the average. Three or four hours a day, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In both 1992 and 1993, you spent some of your time preparing lists with addresses of Muslims, now why?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No. Never lists with Muslim addresses did I make. What for?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's break it down. Did you prepare lists with Muslim names on them?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we have a private session for the witness protection, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I suspect that you'll remember that Miro Kulic carried a white flag while they were walking. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I don't remember that because I was taking part in combat operations in Vitez up there near the church so how could I remember it since I was up there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, because at the time they were walking, you were shooting at them. That's what I'm suggesting, Mr. Buha.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Shooting at whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the people who were moving from the shelter to the building?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: That is not true. Those people were not shot at, and I was in combat operations in Stari Vitez and near the church was engaged in preventing the breakthrough of Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those people who you say were taken to the school, and you say for protection, were going to be taken somewhere else, weren't they; to a meadow called -- and I may get the pronunciation wrong, probably will -- Perina Caira? Tell us about that, please. Why were they going to be taken to such a meadow?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: First time I hear about it. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's go back then. Kulic Miro, what unit was he in?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please? I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Kulic Miro, what unit was he in?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I don't remember, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Well, yes, he was a soldier, but I don't remember what unit he belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he Vitezovi, or Viteska, or was it hard, really, to distinguish between the two?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I think there are several Miro Kulics in Vitez. I don't know which one you mean or any -- there's not one Miroslav Kulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was asking you about him at the beginning, and you seemed to recall him. The person you were then recalling, did he share a barracks with you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But he might have done?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I don't remember. He might have, perhaps, perhaps might have, but I just don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because, of course, you're telling us that your barracks was a small location or a fairly compact location where you would know exactly what's going on; for example, if military or political leaders arrived. Is that the picture of the barracks that we should have?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So wherever you were on the 19th of April -- where were you again?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I never cared who came, why he came. If somebody important came, then I would have been informed. But otherwise, I simply didn't try to keep abreast of who was coming, because I couldn't really watch and record every visit. You understand what I mean. I had my work to do, I had logistics, preparing this for the army and all that. You know what a man responsible for logistics has to do. So I can't remember -- memorise every person and keep track of who's coming, who's going. I really can't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where were you on the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: 19th of April, I was not in the barracks on that day. I was in combat operations up near the church in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Well, easy. I just came to the school on the 16th to fetch some food around 1400, and then I did not come back for another 15 or 17 days because I was supplying a part of our unit up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Back to the general topic. With this small or comparatively small barracks, if there had been any incident where people had been taken out to be shot or had been stopped by forces outside their control, you'd have heard about it, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The soldiers from your barracks might do things like that and it wouldn't be communicated, it wouldn't be discussed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No, nothing like that was done, as far as I know. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to Ahmici itself. Where were you on the night of the 15th and, more important, how can you remember where you were?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I can remember. On the 15th of April, I was in the hall. After I finished and distributed the food for that evening, then in the gymnasium I played football. It was just warming up. I was playing with other soldiers. That night, we played football until midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. And this is in the barracks, in the hall of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And are you telling the Judges that there were no preparations for the deployment of troops later that night or the following day in your barracks at all?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: We did not have the slightest about anything; nor could one expect anything like that or prepare for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you would tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Well, that evening, like any other evening, or the evening when I would have some free time on my hands, we would play football or touch ball or, rather, sports, just physical training and such like, and after that we would go to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened on the night of the 15th/16th? Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Well, like any other night, what could happen? We played football, had a couple of drinks, some beer, and went to bed. What could happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The following morning, you woke up entirely normally or were you woken by anything? Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: In the morning hours, around 6.00, between 5.00 and 6.00, we were woken up by gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where was that all coming from?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Well, it was deafening. It came from all sides, it came from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was attacking whom?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Muslim forces were attacking the town of Vitez, all parts, all parts in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you had heard nothing until then?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Nothing until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You had heard Dubravica -- so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I suffered a shock, a surprise, because we always prepared ourselves together for the front lines for the fighting against the Serbs, and then suddenly something like that. I was really aghast, I was shocked, I was surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course Dubravica is on the Ahmici side of Vitez, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Looking at the road, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So deployments of troops in the direction of Ahmici would have to pass Dubravica if they didn't actually originate at Dubravica; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No. There was no deployment of troops, as far as Vitezovi are concerned, for Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, after all this was over in your small community, you must have discussed what happened at Ahmici. Tell us what did happen, according to what was told to you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: That we talked about it only late in the day. I said -- I asked, "What could it have been that the Muslim forces attacked the HVO members there and that open fighting broke out?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's what you said. But you must have heard from, what, the Viteska Brigade members that were there? Who was it at Ahmici that spoke to you about it; Viteskas?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I did not talk about it to anyone who had been there. We simply heard the story from people who were moving about, from troops who moved about. I asked, "What happened?" and I heard in Stari Vitez -- next to the church is where I heard it -- that in Ahmici, gunfire started and fighting, and the Muslim forces had attacked HVO forces and that the fighting had broken out. And then fighting also began up there in Vitez, and my unit went up to Vitez. And I went together with them, because I was supplying the above-mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you say that somebody told you that the Muslim forces had attacked the HVO forces in Ahmici. It will help us to know who it was who told you that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us who it was.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Some civilians who were moving around, they just came up, and that is how I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, later on in this small community, you must have discovered that a large number of innocent civilians, women and children, and their cattle and so on, had all been killed at Ahmici and their houses burned. What were you told about that, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Well, all sorts of rumours circulated about. I was not down there. I don't know what and how it happened. I was not present. There were all sorts of stories that this is how it was and that's how it was. I cannot claim anything, because I was not there. And in the course of fighting, such things can also happen. I can understand, I mean, when there is fighting going on, that somebody gets -- people can get killed, even people that are innocent. But I do not have any facts at my disposal. I was not present there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go back to the 19th, a couple of days later after Ahmici. Just tell us, by the way, who is Anto Pavelic, or to be precise, who was he?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Anto Pavelic was a leader of the Ustasha movement in World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that a name by which you called yourself from time to time, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Never in my life; nor would I use that name to call myself that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to ask you finally this question about the rounding up of the Muslims. By the time they got to the meadow -- you remember the meadow I described to you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No, I don't remember any meadows.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think I gave a name to you, and I thought you recognised it. I'll have to find the name again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You did mention it, and he said he hadn't heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the time they got to the meadow, were you there shooting at them again?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I don't know anything about any meadows. I wasn't there, so I don't know what you're referring to when you're saying that -- a meadow and shooting at them. I was in Stari Vitez, by the church. That's where I was deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's deal now with your role as logistics. What rank were you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I was the -- in terms of formation establishment, I was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Just tell us what logistics covered at the time you were dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Can you please clarify the question and say what the logistics was supposed to do or what it did? I'm not sure about the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What you did, as a logistics officer in the material time, please, so that we have a picture of your job and life.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: At that time, my task was the equipment, food stocks and other supplies for the troops. I had to deliver them on time. And those were the things, for the most part. We had three or four people, and the men had to have everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That job doesn't necessarily involve your having immediate and advanced contact with the officers making decisions about the deployment of troops and things like that, because they could make their decisions and then they could simply tell you what was required logistically. What I want to know is this: Did you as a matter of fact have regular contact with your superior officers so that you were aware when plans were made and deployment to be effected and so on?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No. I was just doing my work as a logistics officer, and as far as any other operations taking or retreating from lines and things like that, I was not involved in that. I was just involved in my work as a logistics man and followed the orders issued to me by my commander, Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you've expressed an opinion or an answer or given evidence about to whom Darko Kraljevic would respond. From what you've told us, you can't know one way or another whether he would respond to the orders of a senior military man or a politician or to both, can you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: That is correct. That is correct. He did not follow anyone else's orders, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You misunderstood my question, with my mistake, I'll come back to it. From what you've told us about your work as a logistics officer, and the fact that you weren't involved with the other officers when they were making fundamental decisions, from what you've told us about your position, you're, in fact, unable to say whether Darko Kraljevic responded to orders from a senior military officer or whether, in fact, he responded to orders from a politician. He may have done, you can't possibly know.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Knowing Darko Kraljevic for a long time, I doubt, in fact, I can claim rather than doubt knowing his behaviour. I don't know that he -- I don't very much know, in fact. He did not receive any orders from anyone and follow them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What is it in someone's whatever it may be, personality, that stops them from responding to the orders of a politician, for example?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not for him to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you also expressed an opinion about Cerkez. Again, you don't know one way or another from whom Cerkez took his instructions, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I cannot know from whom Cerkez received orders, nor was I interested in that. I was only interested in my work to get it done on time, and properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From your particular perspective and with the limitations that were on you, are you able to help us at all with how Vitezovi operations were coordinated with other HVO Vitezska Brigade operations. Can you help us with how that happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: If there was such coordination, our commander, if he had any communications, I don't know how he did it, I don't even know whether there was any coordination. No. I only did my job. I was not interested in anything else just as I do today. I just go about my business, and I'm not interested in other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't, at the moment, deal with the detailed matters that I said I would have difficulties with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't follow this. You have the evidence of Mr. Breljas which is being contradicted. I don't know what else it is you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps I can explain it briefly in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could the witness just wait outside a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In private session, perhaps, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.50 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Buha, the war, the fighting, was it an occasion for you to sometimes profit for yourself? Were you able to make a profit for yourself from time to time in the war?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I never tried to do it, nor would I ever do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, we've had evidence, and it's Exhibit 332.2 -- it's a small matter but it goes back to the 5th of February, 1993 -- of your seizing a hunting rifle and being reported on that by a witness, the rifle belonging to someone called Zihad Pezer. Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then let's move swiftly forward in time, and I'll return to that topic a little later. The man Breljas, as you were subsequently to discover, was known to senior members of the Vitezovi before Ahmici and the 16th of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No, it is not correct. Nobody ever knew that man until the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to suggest to you that he was on the payroll certainly from March. Do you allow that as a possibility?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to what you say is the incident at the gas station. Am I right in thinking that this is the gas station on the way out from Vitez in the direction of Ahmici, past Dubravica; is that where the gas station is?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No. That gas station is to the right of Vitez towards Travnik on the new road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you telling us that you saw him being arrested or that you heard about it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I did not see him being arrested. I was told that later on, on the 16th, when I came to the barracks in Dubravica, the lads that arrested him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What day was he arrested, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: On the 16th, around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I can accept that he was by a gas station on the 16th, and indeed when he gave evidence to the Judges, he told them about that, and this was the gas station which had been fought over and which had been taken by the Vitezovi. Is it right that the gas station, where he was apparently found, was one that had been taken over by the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes, the Vitezovi held that gas station, and as the lads -- the lads who captured him at the time, that was where they found him, where they came upon him, some hundred metres beyond the gas station. He looked suspicious to them, and that is why they took him to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, again I must suggest you are wrong about that and that what he did was to go from the gas station or from the area of the gas station to the commander called Plavcic. There was a commander called Plavcic, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes, Plavcic did exist, but he did not go anywhere because he was captured and taken into custody. He never went anywhere except as a captive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that he was at that time above the gas station, and that's where some translation skills were used by Breljas, because there was some British soldiers looking for a girl there. Now, does that make -- does that sound familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it was later on that day, on the 16th, it would appear to be, that he went -- he, Breljas, went back to the barracks and stayed there until the evening?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Breljas was arrested on that day, on the 16th, and he was kept under custody in the school nonstop amongst the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How was it, then, that a man you say was in custody suddenly became an accepted member of this special group of fighting men? How did that suddenly come about?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: He did not become that immediately. First he was kept under surveillance, and it was only later that he became a member of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now that evening, the 16th of April, where were you that evening? You probably told us and it's my mistake for missing it. Where were you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I already told you, at 1400 in the afternoon, I came to get the supplies for the unit that evening, and then for the next 17 or 19 days, I was in Stari Vitez, next to the church on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So, first of all, were you there, you say, when Breljas was brought to the barracks or did he come to the barracks apparently after you had already left?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I saw Breljas in the barracks at 1400. When I came to get the materiel and food and whatever people -- men needed, I came there to take it with me to Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But this is clear: If there was a meeting that evening, on the evening of the 16th, in the barracks involving Kordic, you wouldn't be able to help us one way or another because you weren't there yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: All I can say is there could not be any meeting, since Plavcic and all my men and Mr. Darko Kraljevic were in Vitez together with me at the front line, at the defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So this much is clear about Plavcic: He was certainly at liberty on the 16th even if he was subsequently himself taken captive, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Plavcic was never captured. Plavcic operated with me next to the church. Nobody was freed then. Everybody who was freed went back and we went to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you've said whether Kordic would have been seen at the barracks. I must inquire of you whether Kordic was careful sometimes about being -- careful about being seen perhaps both at the barracks and as I must ask you at the restaurant or coffee house when you were taking lists of Muslim people. Let's deal with it in two stages. Were there occasions when, to your knowledge, Kordic visited that restaurant used by the troops and did so quite discreetly?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No. I never saw Kordic, Mr. Kordic to come to that restaurant or some meetings. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in the course of the lunchtime, which was, I'm sorry, a little extended, entirely my fault, in the course of that lunchtime, have you been able to think back to anything that you did that might have looked like you were gathering names of residents, perhaps particularly Muslim names? Have you been able to think of anything that might have been misinterpreted like that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No, I never did it, nor would I do that, nor was that part of my job, of the job that I had with the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll move on then, and I've only got a few more questions to ask you and it is these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Nice. I wish to ask this of the witness. Could it be that Mr. Kordic went to the barracks? Could he have visited the barracks without being noticed, without being seen by the witness? In other words, could the witness see all the people who would come to the barracks, and this -- could it have been with --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: To begin with, there was security around the barracks. Nobody could enter unannounced and unobserved. And if such a personality, such a public figure came to us, it would have been a privilege for me to see him there. However, he did not, unfortunately, he did not come, and I have repeated it already several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But of course if he decided to come without any fanfare and to come privately, that would be a matter for him. He could achieve it, couldn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. No, nobody could achieve that. Nobody could achieve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You mean if a senior and important person like Mr. Kordic arrived and said he wanted his meeting to be secret and to be kept from all the soldiers, people would not obey him and they would let it be known that he was there. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. Nobody can enter. Nobody can enter unannounced without the men around the barracks knowing about it, nobody, nobody whoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you certainly accept that if he came on the 16th in the evening, you wouldn't know about it yourself because you weren't there. And you weren't there, on your account, for many days to come, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I was not in the barracks, but Mr. Kraljevic and other commanders were with me next to the church so there would be nobody that he could talk to there. That is logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move forward and returning to the topic of whether the war benefited you financially, personally. First of all, do you remember any incidence of cars or engines from Siroki Brijeg that you were in a position to sell and make money out of?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I never did that. I wouldn't do that. I simply was not brought up that way to do things like that, especially in a war when people can be put before the firing squad for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Breljas took over from you as logistics officer, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Correct. Correct. Because he had access everywhere. He simply invented that I had stolen something and since he knew how to phone up to people, that is what happened. However, after some days, they took me back because they had run short of food and everything. In addition to Breljas, there were five more. Whatever stocks we had were sold. Breljas did that and then I headed to purchase these things again, and I continued to do my job, and he was transferred to the IPD.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So it was not a case of his working with you in the logistics. He had you sacked because he caught you thieving. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: He never caught me thieving, he -- yes, sir, he did work with me, but he wanted to help on his own, to distribute food to some individuals. But to me it is vital for soldiers to have it and that is where we disagreed, but he somehow had a say with the commander and that is how it came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will suggest it wasn't a say with the commander, but he actually caught you doing what you had been doing perhaps throughout this conflict which was to look after yourself at the expense of others. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No. That could never be correct. My soldiers in the barracks would have passed judgement on me if I ever did anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then even later on towards the end of 1993 and into 1994, the Deputy Commander Vinac, with you, were abusing the stores that should have gone to the soldiers and selling them on the black market because you could make money out of it.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No, it's a lie. It's purely and simply a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have any experience at about the same time of Muslims being taken out and forced to work at the front line?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When I say the experience, did you see any members of the Vitezovi doing that or any of the members of the other local brigades doing that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No, I did not. I did not see that. But where I was, with my Vitezovi, we dug our own trenches because nobody else would do it better than we could do it and we did not trust anyone else to do it for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness just see, arising from questions asked by Mr. Kovacic, very briefly, Exhibit 1380. It's the second sheet of the English version when it comes everybody's way, and it is also the second sheet, I think. Yes, it's the very top of the second sheet of the B/C/S version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked questions about someone called Dragan Vinac and about people exaggerating their tours of duty for some reason. What you're looking at is the second page in B/C/S of a report actually prepared by, as we can see on our page nine, Major Dragan Vinac as he then was. If you look at the top of the second page, you're looking at a -- two lines that reads, "The commanders of the team were Captain Berislav Sapina and Captain Dragan Vinac. The team operated in the vicinity of Stolac." Do you see that right at the top of the second sheet? I hope I have it right. Now, if you come back to the previous page, and if the Chamber will just cast it's eye out a little further on, I think, page two, and it says this, "Following the order of Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic issued on the 14th of October, the commander of the PPN Vitezovi, Darko Kraljevic, issued an order about sending 60 soldiers of the PPN to Grude." And then it goes on to say, "The commanders of the team were Captain Sapina and Captain Dragan Vinac." I just want you to confirm, Mr. Buha, you're not suggesting, are you, that Dragan Vinac was not an operating member of the Vitezovi in October of 1992 are you, or anything like that? For it's clear that he was.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: I'll tell you. Yes, men went to Stolac and part of the PPN Vitezovi went to Stolac, to the Stolac front to fight the Serbs because that was the Serb front line. That is the defence of the Croat lands, that is Bosnia-Herzegovina against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are not being asked about the men. You are asked about Captain Vinac.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes, Captain Vinac. Captain Vinac was and -- led that group to Stolac, to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help us with this, Mr. Buha, so that it's clear. Did Mr. Breljas accuse you of stealing the stores?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes, he did accuse me of stealing the stores.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And selling it on the black market?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what particular stores were they?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Food. It was food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what happened as a result of the accusation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: On the basis of these accusations, Commander Kraljevic came, found facts, realised that I had too many responsibilities and said, "Josip, no problem. You are going to the front line. Breljas will take over this from you." and some five or six days later, all the stores that existed disappeared. There was Breljas and five more men and it all vanished so that Commander Kraljevic brought me back to purchase food and medicines and all the rest that the troops might need. And it was not difficult for me to find that at all and I did, and I stayed doing that job again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And as a result of the accusation, was there bad feeling between you and Breljas?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes. We had an argument, a verbal one; nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Very briefly, a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Buha, you were asked about the road from Vitez to Ahmici and onward. The school at Dubravica, the elementary school and its yard are not on the main road from Vitez to Ahmici, are they?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No, no, no, the school is not by the main road. It is about 200 metres from the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And in view of the buildings and houses next to the road, could one see, from the yard at the school at Dubravica, who was moving down that road towards Ahmici from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No, it is impossible to because there are trees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You've just answered the questions of His Honour, and let me just shed complete light on it, because I'm not sure the transcript put it right. This gas station which is called Hvidra at the moment, it is on the roundabout road which from Vitez goes to Travnik and Novi Travnik; is that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So this is not the other side of the road towards Busovaca and Ahmici, looking from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Looking from Vitez, if we take that road, both the school and Ahmici are on the same side as the gas station, that they are on the same side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. But unlike the school in Dubravica by which the road to Ahmici goes, the gas station is on the other side of the road towards Travnik?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You said today that Darko Kraljevic, your commander, basically did not heed to anyone; that is what you told us today?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you know anything about an incident when Darko Kraljevic allegedly came uninvited to a meeting where Mr. Blaskic and Mr. Kordic were and then did something to them or said something to them; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP BUHA
utterances.text: No, I do not know that. I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Your Honours, that is all. Thank you, Mr. Buha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buha, for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. It's now concluded. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness is Slavko Pavlovic. We have submitted two affidavits in corroboration of his testimony. He will have one videotape exhibit, which we'll show a very short snippet of, and we have a transcript of the videotape in Croatian and a translation in English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The videotape will be Exhibit D215/1, and the transcript, D215A/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, just so the position is clear, the transcript that we have produced is a transcript of a news programme, following which I believe the press conference of April the 15th was shown again. That's previously been marked as an exhibit, Z665, and a transcript of that press conference has already been made part of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please state your name for the Court?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Slavko Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a few matters of detail about your personal background, sir. I'll take you through those very quickly. I believe you were born on September the 18th, 1956, in the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You are a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a Bosnian Croat by ethnicity, and a Roman Catholic by religion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a Bosnian Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that you received your primary education in Vitez, your secondary education in Tuzla, and that you attended the University of Sarajevo, graduating from that institution in 1978 with a degree in music.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And from the end of 1992 until June of 1993, you performed the job of director of TV Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I believe, sir, that you are married, you have two children, that your family lives in Vitez, and that both you and your wife have essentially lived in Vitez all your life.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You currently work as a music teacher in that town, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as a music teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Pavlovic, as the director at TV Vitez, did you become familiar with the broadcasts and interviews given by Bosnian Croat politicians during the civil war that were later broadcast on TV Vitez, and if so, could you tell the Judges exactly how you became aware of those and what connection you had with their rebroadcast, if any?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, yes. And as the director of TV Vitez, a freshman journalist who worked there who was gathering material for what we needed, obviously as a manager, I reviewed all the materials that arrived, including those press conference materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And were those materials reviewed and edited to be broadcast later in the day over your TV station?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, all daily events that occurred in the town of Vitez we would then broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And amongst the press conferences given in Vitez or Busovaca, did you ever have occasion to see press conferences that were attended by local political figures such as Mr. Dario Kordic, Mr. Ignac Kostroman, Mr. Anto Valenta, or others?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: As a manager, I did not attend any of the press conferences. But if I can anticipate your question later, I was not present at the conference attended by Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But the cameramen employed by your TV station presumably were in attendance and actually recording these conferences?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, I believe that we have made you aware of certain claims made in this case that Mr. Kordic supposedly held a press conference on April the 15th, 1993, in which it is claimed he stated on television that, "his troops" were awaiting orders to attack Bosnian Muslims. Could you tell the Court, Mr. Pavlovic, was any such statement made, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No. I can remember that press conference and Mr. Kordic. It was a very significant day for our town and the wider region.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, recordings of this press conference were actually played by your TV station on April the 15th, 1993; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And we've already shown you, I think, the Prosecution exhibits, the recordings which have already been admitted into evidence in this case, marked Z665, and obviously as the Court recalls, this press conference concerned the kidnapping of Zivko Totic, the commander of the Jure Francetic Brigade, and the killing of Commander Totic's bodyguards. Do you have any knowledge, sir, of any other press conferences attended by Mr. Kordic on that day or which were broadcast on that day, or the next day, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, except for that conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps you've already answered this question, but let me make it absolutely clear. Did Mr. Kordic -- did your TV station broadcast any other statements or speeches given by Mr. Kordic on either April the 15th or April the 16th, 1993, other than this press conference, a copy of which has already been introduced into evidence as Exhibit Z665?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. No. But let me try to elaborate on what you asked before, whether he stated that -- whether the troops were on the ready. He did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court how many times this videotape was actually broadcast over your TV station on April the 15th, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was broadcast twice in the morning hours, and what we always did with press conferences of any kind, it would be rebroadcast in the show called "Slikom Na Sliku", "Picture And Picture".

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I believe that a news programme was broadcast by TV Vitez on April the 15th at around 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as every day at 7.00 p.m., TV Vitez always did a 7.00 newscast.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I would like to show a brief extract from this news programme just for identification purposes, and that's already been marked as Exhibit 215/1, and the translations and transcripts have been marked as D215A/1. I wonder if I could ask the usher to help out the witness by putting the programme on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters also be provided with copies of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think they have been. Apparently, Your Honour, we fouled up. There are some additional copies here for the interpreters, if they need them. I think there are four separate segments, or a number of segments, Mr. President. We only propose to show one of them, just for identification purposes, because the programme speaks for itself. Yes. If we could have the videotape shown now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Dear viewers of TV Vitez, good evening. The most important news is the serious crime that was committed today around 8.00 a.m. in Zenica when the vehicle in which Mr. Zivko Totic, the commander of the Jure Francetic Brigade, was travelling towards the HVO command in Zenica was attacked. The commander's escorts, Ivica Vidovic, Anto Zaric, Marko and Tihomir, were treacherously killed in that attack. A passerby, whose identity is yet unknown, was also killed. The commander of the Jure Francetic Brigade, Mr. Zivko Totic, was abducted, and his whereabouts and fate are unknown. According to the latest information we have received, there is no shooting in Zenica, but the situation is very tense. In connection with this, a special press conference was held today in Busovaca that you could have watched earlier. For all those among you who were not able to see this press conference, we will air it again after the "Slikom Na Sliku" telecast. A proclamation by the Central Bosnia Operative Zone was read at the conference, and we will show it in its entirety during this newscast.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... unless, of course, the Court wants to see it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pavlovic, is that an accurate copy of the news programme that was aired on April the 15th, 1993, just after Commander Totic's kidnapping?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Could you just tell the Court, other than the news programme that we've just had marked as an exhibit and the press conference that was videotaped and aired on April the 15th, what other programming did TV Vitez show on April the 15th, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I think that very simply every day, including the 15th, the programming was filled by EuroSport broadcasts, old movies, and the only other thing we could do, with the help of our friends, was to rebroadcast "Slikom Na Sliku" and also to broadcast news. In other words, every day was about the same, including the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in April of 1993, is it correct to say that TV Vitez only produced its own news programmes or videotapes of press conferences that were aired later, and apart from these types of news broadcasts, the only other programming broadcast by TV Vitez was produced originally by other TV stations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: What we broadcast, we broadcast material which we had available. And our equipment was practically for amateurs, and the only thing we could produce were the local news in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Pavlovic, as you said, you've lived in the Vitez area all of your life.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever heard that Mr. Kordic supposedly made a statement after the Ahmici blockade incident in October of 1992 to the effect that Ahmici would be burned to the ground, or would pay a dear price, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No. And in October, I was not the manager yet, but I would have been informed about it at the time when I assumed the duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever see such a programme on which such statements were made yourself?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I take it that you've not heard about any such statements ever having been made by Mr. Kordic or by anybody else for that matter along the lines I've just recited to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I just said so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do those kinds of comments sound to you like the kinds of comments that Mr. Kordic would have made from your knowledge of the news broadcasts or the press conferences that he actually did speak at?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: You will have an opportunity, Your Honours, and everybody else, to see a tape of the press conference and you will see that he was a very moderate man. This is how I knew him before all these things happened. So my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much indeed, sir. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pavlovic. The Defence of Mr. Cerkez, which I represent along with Mr. Kovacic, is going to ask you several questions. Please try to answer them to the best of your recollection. Mr. Pavlovic, you said that you were a music teacher?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But that in December of 1992, you assumed the post of the manager of TV Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would like you to very briefly describe how you took over this position?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: It's very simple. I will be brief. As a professor of music, I had previously worked in Travnik and I taught music, but there were a lot of interruptions in my commute. A lot of time I had to stop going to Travnik because I used to travel daily between Vitez and Travnik. Then the refugees started arriving and more and more people. The population was swelling and we were feeling more and more unsafe. And first we started village guards or home guards, then people said that I shouldn't be doing this, and I wanted to join for the safety of my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here. When you say the village guards or home guards, you mean the organised security of the apartment building where you lived?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then Mr. Santic offered you the job of manager of the local TV station in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, before these events in December of 1992, what type of TV programmes could be viewed in the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, the only relay in -- which was in Kruscica, I believe it was called, the Muslims that took control of it. Apparently there were two channels there, but I did not manage to get one of them for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, and in order for the Trial Chamber to gain the right picture, is it true that the relay which was sending the signals to Vitez was somehow taken over by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that they simply refused to provide the services of this relay to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I was authorised by Mr. Ivica Santic, with the representative of the Bosnian people, Suad Salkic. I tried everything. It was such the time and we wanted to try everything. This relay was supposed to have been used by all ethnic groups who were there, three or four or five who were there, that nobody would have special advantage, but he said that he was not competent to discuss this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So in other words, this attempt of yours to negotiate failed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the Bosniak was the only one using this relay facility in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Then you build your own relay on an amateur basis?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and this is what we still use to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the power that this relay had?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: My friends and colleagues and staff, Kurebac [phoen] and others, said it was about five watts which is very little. I am a musician. I don't know exactly how much that is, but anybody can check this because the facility is still there as it was. It could only cover the town of Vitez and its surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Mr. Pavlovic, the local TV Vitez studio was -- had its premises in the local theatre?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And before that, it was in the private apartment of Minister Gudin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So in addition to the TV studio there was other offices there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was. The political party had its office there and there was a cafe and there was also the headquarters there when I arrived in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You're referring to the municipal staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said you employed new, young journalists who were amateurs. Mr. Pavlovic, do you remember at that time whether the daughters of Mr. Hasan Salibasic worked, and their names were Soncica and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I said there was one name which was Vildana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In any event, those two girls were of Muslim background?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of those still works for a Croat businessman. But yes, people worked regularly there. Nobody could dream what would happen next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you or anybody else exert any pressure on them or any other Muslim employees?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No. Everything was very correct and fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know whether these ethnic Muslims were giving trouble, were given trouble by their fellow compatriots for speaking in the Croat dialect?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I believe at that time still not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And later? If you don't know, we can move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether later they had any trouble?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, it is said that you lived in a newer section of Vitez. How about your parents?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I was born near the mosque in Stari Vitez which is the part of -- section of town called Mahala. My father was also born there. I am not sure about my grandfather, but we -- the family has been there for 200 to 300 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So it is -- a part of town with predominantly Bosnian or Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Pavlovic, what happened to you on the morning of the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: It was a disaster. As the TV station manager, I could not cover the 500 metres from where I lived to where I went to work because of all the shelling. It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As the leading media person or information person in town, did you know anything about these events, that there would be a conflict on that day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I've always wanted to say this. If -- I will slow down so that it can be interpreted. Even -- I was a musician, it's maybe too much to call me a media person. If somebody wanted to bring something to the TV Vitez, and this is what happened on the 16th. My parents lived in the town of Vitez and Their Honours and everybody else who is here are wise people. They could assume that I would first go for my parents. I would not want them to be in Mahala on that day, but they stayed in Mahala for a whole year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you were not able to have any contact with them for a full year until the cease-fire was signed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, some people went to Mahala, they said that it would last a very short period of time. They said, "Franjo, you will be able to go to church in five or six days." And then after a month or two, they said it would be all right. But it was not all right, and I did not see my father for many months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you had no information what was all going on with your parents in Stari Vitez, in Old Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, we did all kinds of things. I don't know if it reached CNN but we did all kinds of things to try and find out whether they were still alive. My father, as an elderly man, we were all in a good mood, he always sang a song, a particular song, they're referring to the home and family. And he -- we could -- we would be able to hear that he was 500 or 600 metres away but there was no -- we'd never heard him or we never saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Then I understand you saw your father from afar?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mother I did not see on that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Pavlovic, did you ever hear in what circumstances did they live during that year in Stari Vitez while in -- while surrounded?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we learned that afterwards. We heard it from Helda, who was an elderly man, and his son Besim. They spent in the cellar only four months. Our house is only some 50 metres from there, yet they never did go to our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So your parents were taken from their own house and put in a cellar, rather like a prison, where they spent four months?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: No, not only they, there were 20 or 30 people of Croat ethnicity as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So they were kept in that cellar, citizens in Stari Vitez who were of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, our neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, you told us in the beginning that at the request of Ivica Santic in December of 1992, you took over the job of the manager and if I am correct, you held that post until June 1993, and what happened then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was then really fed up with everything and I asked Ivica once again to send me to the defence front line, to the trenches with my brothers, because I was suffering such pressure. I simply wanted to be with my brothers. Because I was in the television, and the armchair is the armchair and the trench is a trench, and you know how things are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And your three brothers were members of the HVO at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you joined them then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And where, what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "what position"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, you told us that you went into a trench?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Next to the cathedral, next to our church, St. George in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And that was the area which was held by the main unit of the Vitez Brigade, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.
